title: Blessings, Curses, and a Covenant Remembered
summary: God sets before Israel the consequences of the covenant. If they obey, he will send rain and harvest, peace and victory, and he will live among them as their God. If they reject him, he will bring disease, drought, wild animals, war, famine, and finally exile, each stage more severe than the last. Yet even in exile, if they confess their sin and humble their hearts, God will remember his covenant with Abraham, Isaac, and Jacob and will not destroy them.
story: Chapter 26 brings the Holiness Code, and in a sense the whole of the laws given at Sinai, to a close. The final verse names them as "the statutes, ordinances, and laws" that God established through Moses on Mount Sinai (verse 46), and chapter 27 is an appendix on vows. Ancient covenants often ended with blessings for keeping them and curses for breaking them, and this chapter does the same. It looks far ahead: past the conquest of Canaan, through centuries of life in the land, to a time when Israel would be scattered among the nations. Deuteronomy 28 contains a parallel set of blessings and curses, and the history books from Joshua to Kings, as well as the prophets, read Israel's story through these two chapters.
historical:
Treaties between ancient kings and their vassals commonly ended with blessings and curses invoked by the gods. Hittite treaties of the second millennium BC follow this pattern, and so do the vassal treaties of the Assyrian king Esarhaddon from 672 BC, whose long lists of curses (drought, famine, disease, wild beasts, and even parents eating their children) resemble those of Leviticus 26 and Deuteronomy 28. The Code of Hammurabi also closes with blessings on rulers who uphold it and curses on those who alter it. Israel's covenant followed a form its neighbors would have recognized, with one great difference: the covenant partner was the LORD himself, not a human king.

The curses were not merely theoretical. When the Arameans besieged Samaria, mothers ate their children (2 Kings 6:28-29), and Lamentations 4:10 records the same horror in the Babylonian siege of Jerusalem before its fall in 587 or 586 BC. The exile scattered Judah among the nations, and 2 Chronicles 36:21 says the land then enjoyed its Sabbaths, closely echoing verses 34 and 35. Scholars who date the Holiness Code early see these as prophetic warnings later fulfilled; many who date it to the exile see the chapter as shaped by the experience it describes. Readers on both sides agree that exilic and post-exilic Israel read it as an explanation of their suffering and a ground for hope.
cultural:
Israel's farming depended entirely on rain. Unlike Egypt, watered by the Nile, or Mesopotamia with its rivers, the hill country of Canaan relied on autumn and spring rains. The image of a sky like iron and ground like bronze (verse 19) described a drought in which nothing fell from above and nothing broke through below. The promises of verses 4 to 10 picture the opposite: harvests so large that threshing runs into grape-picking and grape-picking into sowing, and last year's grain must be cleared out to make room for the new.

The blessings rise to a climax not in food or safety but in God's presence: "I will make My dwelling place among you" and "I will walk among you and be your God, and you will be My people" (verses 11 and 12). The verb for walking is the same one used for God walking in the garden in Genesis 3:8. The phrase about an uncircumcised heart (verse 41) uses circumcision, the physical sign of the covenant, as a picture of an inner life that has not been given to God.
literary: The chapter opens with two summary commands on idols and Sabbaths (verses 1 and 2), then gives blessings (verses 3 to 13) and curses (verses 14 to 39), followed by a turn toward restoration (verses 40 to 45) and a closing summary (verse 46). The curses are far longer than the blessings and are arranged in five rising stages, each introduced by a condition such as "if after all this you will not obey Me" (verses 14, 18, 21, 23, 27). The number seven recurs (verses 18, 21, 24, 28) to mark each escalation. A rare Hebrew word translated hostility runs through the second half: Israel walks in hostility toward God, and God answers in kind. The ending reverses the direction. God remembers his covenant with Jacob, Isaac, and Abraham, listing the patriarchs backward, as if tracing the covenant to its roots.

outline.t: Rising judgments: drought, wild animals, war, and famine
Final judgment: siege, ruin, and exile

doctrines.note: The covenant is a relationship with consequences. Obedience brings blessing and rebellion brings judgment, but the covenant rests finally on God's promise to Abraham, Isaac, and Jacob, which he will remember even when Israel has broken it.
God's judgments come in stages, each meant to turn his people back before the next. The chapter calls them discipline (verse 23), showing that judgment is aimed at repentance before it becomes final.

Verses 40 and 41 describe repentance: confessing one's own sin and the sin of one's ancestors, humbling the heart, and accepting the consequences. God answers such repentance by remembering his covenant.

Even at its darkest, the chapter refuses to end in destruction: "I will not reject or despise them so as to destroy them and break My covenant with them" (verse 44). Israel's hope in exile rested on this promise.

words.note: Berit, covenant: a binding relationship sealed by solemn promises. It appears eight times in this chapter. Israel can break the covenant (verse 15), but God will not break it (verse 44), and he will remember it for their sake (verses 42 and 45).

Qeri, hostility or contrariness, a rare word that appears seven times in this chapter. It may carry a sense of walking by chance or at cross purposes. Israel's hostility toward God is met by God's hostility toward them: the relationship becomes a collision until they repent.

Zakhar, to remember. In the Bible, God's remembering is not recalling something forgotten but acting on a commitment. When God remembered Noah (Genesis 8:1) the waters receded; when he remembers his covenant here, exile will not be the end.

Yasar, to discipline or correct, as a parent corrects a child. Verse 23 frames the escalating judgments as discipline that Israel refuses to accept. The same verb is used in Proverbs for a father's instruction of his son.

christ: Paul quotes the heart of the blessings to the Corinthian church: "I will dwell with them and walk among them, and I will be their God, and they will be My people" (2 Corinthians 6:16, drawing on this chapter and other prophets). Revelation's final vision fulfills it: "Behold, the dwelling place of God is with man, and He will dwell with them" (Revelation 21:3). The New Testament also presents Christ as the one who bore the covenant curse on behalf of those who broke it: "Christ redeemed us from the curse of the law by becoming a curse for us" (Galatians 3:13). Jesus himself wept over Jerusalem and warned of its coming siege and scattering (Luke 19:41-44 and 21:20-24), which happened when Rome destroyed the city in AD 70. And the uncircumcised heart that needed humbling (verse 41) is answered by the promise of a new heart, which Paul describes as a circumcision "of the heart, by the Spirit" (Romans 2:29).

hard.q: Does this chapter mean that suffering is always God's punishment and prosperity always his reward?
hard.a: The chapter does connect obedience with blessing and rebellion with disaster, and some have taken it as a promise that faithful people will prosper and suffering people must have sinned. But the blessings and curses are addressed to Israel as a nation living in the land under the Sinai covenant, and they describe the long-term direction of its life together, not a formula for every individual. Other parts of Scripture refuse the individual reading. Job suffers precisely because he is righteous, many psalms lament the suffering of the innocent, and Jesus rejected the idea that victims of disaster were worse sinners than others (Luke 13:1-5) or that a man born blind was being punished (John 9:3). The New Testament does not promise material prosperity for faithfulness; it promises hardship alongside God's presence. Readers have also found the curses themselves, especially verse 29, deeply disturbing. Interpreters generally understand them as a stark description of what siege and war actually did in the ancient world, set out in advance as a warning meant to turn Israel back before it came to that.

questions: The highest blessing in the chapter is not rain or safety but God living among his people. What do you most hope to receive from God, and how does this chapter reorder that hope?
The judgments escalate in stages, each giving another chance to turn back. Where might God be trying to get your attention through smaller consequences before larger ones?
Verse 40 speaks of confessing both one's own sins and the sins of one's ancestors. What might it mean for a church or a nation to confess the wrongs of past generations?
